metadata.title: Why Classical Physics Failed
metadata.topic: Blackbody radiation, the ultraviolet catastrophe, Planck's reluctant quantization, and Einstein's photon — why classical physics couldn't survive contact with a glowing piece of iron

beats.narration_text: Namaste — I'm Professor Sridhar. Today's chapter: why the physics of 1900 could not survive contact with a glowing piece of iron. The classical prediction was not just wrong. It predicted infinite energy pouring out of every warm object in this room. That one number is where quantum mechanics begins.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Namaste, Prof Sridhar'; ask types itself
output lands: 'Not a lot of energy. Infinite energy.'

props.command: Why did classical physics predict infinite energy from a warm object?
output: Classical physics didn't get "a lot of energy."

beats.narration_text: Act one. The ultraviolet catastrophe — and the fix nobody wanted to believe.

props.headline: The Ultraviolet Catastrophe
props.topic: Why the classical count of modes runs to infinity

beats.narration_text: Heat iron in a forge and it glows red, then orange, then yellow-white — any iron, any temperature, the same spectrum. By 1900 that curve had been measured to within a percent. The best theory of the day did not predict it badly. It predicted infinite energy.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: iron heating red -> yellow-white while the classical prediction runs to infinity

beats.narration_text: Count the field's modes in a hot cavity — pure geometry, nobody disputes it. Give each mode its classical share of energy and multiply. At low frequency the match is perfect. But the mode count grows without limit, and classical physics gives every one of those modes the same energy. The curve does not level off. It runs to infinity.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: Rayleigh-Jeans curve diverging at high frequency

beats.narration_text: Planck was not trying to invent quantum mechanics — he was trying to fit a curve. The only fit that worked assumed the wall's oscillators could not hold just any energy. Only discrete steps: zero, h-nu, two h-nu, three h-nu. Do that, and the curve bends over exactly where the data bends over — matching classical physics at low frequency, and falling to zero at high frequency instead of exploding.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: Planck distribution overlaid on Rayleigh-Jeans, boxed formula

beats.narration_text: Put a number on the failure. At a tungsten-lamp temperature, in the ultraviolet, classical physics and Planck's formula disagree by a factor of ten to the twenty. Not twice as bright. Not off by half. Twenty orders of magnitude — the whole disagreement traced to one ratio, h-nu over k-B-T, and where that ratio crosses one is exactly where quantum effects take over.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: golden-test number reveal — the 10^-20 ratio, on screen with its own check

beats.narration_text: Act two. A completely different crisis — and the photon that resolved both.

props.headline: One Photon, One Electron
props.topic: The photoelectric effect, and why waves can't explain it

beats.narration_text: Meanwhile, ultraviolet light hitting a metal knocks electrons loose — and every measured detail defies the wave picture. Below a threshold frequency, nothing comes out, at any brightness. Above it, brighter light makes more electrons, never faster ones. And the electrons appear instantly, with no delay to build up energy. A wave should not behave like this.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: three panels — threshold, intensity-vs-count, no time delay

beats.narration_text: Einstein's answer, 1905: light isn't spread continuously at all. It arrives in packets, energy h-nu each, absorbed one photon to one electron. Below threshold, a single photon simply cannot do the job — not almost, not with help from the next one — it cannot, ever. Above threshold, the leftover energy becomes the electron's kinetic energy, and Millikan's own data, for three different metals, traces the same slope: h over e, exactly.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: stopping potential vs frequency, three metals, identical slope

beats.narration_text: Shine 300-nanometer ultraviolet on sodium and you get a stopping potential of 1.85 volts — computed, not measured, straight from h-nu minus the work function. Drop to green light, 546 nanometers, and the photon energy falls a hair below threshold. The result isn't weaker current. It's zero electrons — from a lamp of any brightness you like.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: sodium worked example, UV vs green light contrast

beats.narration_text: Compton's 1923 experiment closed the loop: X-rays scattering off graphite come back at a longer wavelength, exactly as they would bouncing off a particle with momentum h over lambda. Light is not a wave that sometimes acts like a particle. It is one object, always described by a probability wave, whose detections are always discrete. Both descriptions are real — they were never in competition.
beats.new_visual_element: Manim: Compton scattering geometry, longer scattered wavelength, wave-AND-particle synthesis

beats.narration_text: Two quantizations, one chapter. Planck quantized reluctantly — only the wall's oscillators, never the field itself. Einstein quantized on purpose — the field itself, one photon at a time. Millikan spent two years trying to disprove the photon and instead measured Planck's constant: h over e, the same slope for sodium, lithium, and potassium.

artifactLines: Planck quantized reluctantly — the wall's oscillators, never the field.
Einstein quantized on purpose — the field itself, one photon at a time.
Millikan tried to disprove it and measured h instead: h/e = 4.136×10⁻¹⁵ V·s, the same slope across three metals.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick any metal from a work-function table, and a UV wavelength of your own choosing. Ask Claude to compute the photon energy, check whether electrons are emitted at all, and if so, work out the stopping potential. Then ask what happens if you multiply the light's intensity by a thousand — does the stopping potential change? Run it, and see if Claude's answer matches what this chapter just showed you.

props.command: Pick a metal and a UV wavelength. Compute the photon energy, tell me whether photoelectrons are emitted, and if so the stopping potential. Then: if I multiply the light's intensity by 1000, does the stopping potential change? Why or why not?
